Here are observations on both recent sales and market conditions.

Let's discuss our best approach to pricing, timing and strategy.

These are just observations I'm making so we can have a conversation about where we fit.

Of all the recent comparable sales, 648 F Street sits the farthest north.

This was also true of the comps we used when we went to market last April.

Only one recent sale shares our setup: a closed-off lower level plus a carriage house.

Only one sale with our setup.
All sales are south of our location.

Buyers in this price range are, by and large, looking for as many features as they can get out of the main house.

They typically don't give up the features they want in exchange for a lower price. They wait for a home that has the features they are looking for.

Our eventual buyer will likely be a reach-up purchaser who sees value in three different zones.

What buyers notice

How buyers see 648 F Street

Layout

  • Two connected levels; no interior stairs to the lower level
  • HVAC sits where stairs would go
  • The old spiral stair cut into the living room

Features

  • Small primary bath
  • Minimal outdoor space
  • North of East Capitol, toward H Street
Legal rental status

Legal rental status

Lower level

  • Not a legal second unit today
  • Needs separate meters, panel and HVAC, plus a fire separation
  • About 5–6 months plus construction

Carriage house

  • Not on a named alley
  • RF-1 zoning makes a third unit unlikely
  • STR license is not a Certificate of Occupancy

Current Market Condition Statistics

Low inventory has been the main thing holding prices up through the big jump in rates.

Inventory is now above 2019 levels

2019 is the baseline because it was the last normal market before inventory got tight.

If inventory levels rise through the spring, that will place downward pressure on prices.

Number of sellers jumps to a 6-year high

About 1.53 million U.S. sellers in the market vs. about 972,000 buyers.

The 10-year Treasury yield drives mortgage rates, and it will likely stay elevated because of inflation and the national debt.

10-Year Treasury yield

Annual average, 2011–2025 (Federal Reserve via FRED). Latest: 5.00% on Oct 26, 2026.

Federal debt held by the public

$0.3 trillion in 1970. $30 trillion today. $56 trillion projected by 2036.

Trillions of dollars, fiscal year-end. Sources: OMB and Treasury via FRED; CBO projections (Feb 2026).

30-year fixed mortgage rate

From 16.63% in 1981 to 2.96% in 2021. Today: 7.32%.

Annual average, 1980–2025; latest weekly rate Oct 22, 2026. Source: Freddie Mac PMMS.

Historically, today's rates aren't high. The issue is how fast they jumped from an artificially low point that many people came to see as normal. The market is adjusting very gradually.

DC has long been an insulated market because of the government, but that has changed.

Federal jobs in the D.C. region: lowest in 30 years

Pending home sales in September hit their lowest level in 25 years.

Around 5.5 million a year before 2022. About 4 million today.

Looking ahead

Looking ahead

Prices

Likely lower in 12 months

Inventory

If it loosens up, prices drop more

Nobody knows.

I can't predict what the market will do. I see more headwinds than tailwinds. Baby boomers staying put and low inventory are what's holding prices up. If inventory ever breaks loose, I expect more downward pressure on prices. More sellers are watching these headwinds, and many will likely test the market this spring.

Someone could pay more. The question is, what are the odds?

Most likely70%
Possible20%
Least likely10% or less

Imperfect properties perform differently in a seller's market than in a buyer's market. When the market is hot, buyers make more compromises. When it isn't, they make fewer.

This is the data as I see it. It's here to talk through together, honestly, not to argue for a number.
